<a id="align-elements"></a>

### Align elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** line these elements up with one reference element, axis by axis - or line MEP runs up by their top, bottom or centre at one height.

Moves elements so they share one reference element's position along whichever axes are asked for - *"get these diffusers on the same line"*, *"line the equipment up with that one"*. Each axis is chosen separately, so aligning in X leaves every element's own Y and Z alone. **It aligns each element's own position point, which for a duct or pipe is its MIDPOINT, not an end.** Two runs of different lengths aligned this way share a centre, and their ends do not line up. That is the right answer for equipment and the wrong one for somebody who meant "make the ends meet" - and the difference is invisible until it is looked at. **MEP runs by their top, bottom or centre (version 2, 2026-11-01).** ALIGN_MEP_ELEVATION was merged in. Give `edge` - top, bottom or centre - and `targetZ`, a height in millimetres, instead of a reference: each duct, pipe, tray or conduit is moved up or down so that edge lands on the height, its half-height read from its OWN size, so a 600 mm duct and a 100 mm pipe genuinely share a soffit. The insertion point of an MEP run is its centreline, so making centrelines equal leaves the tops and bottoms apart - which is exactly what a coordinated corridor needs to be equal. A run whose size cannot be read is in `noSize` and not moved; something not curve-based is in `notCurveBased`. Insulation is NOT included - the bare service size. A sloped run's midpoint lands on the height and its slope is kept. Every move is read back. Version 2's proof is owed; the card is DRAFT. **"SOFFIT" MEANS TWO DIFFERENT JOBS AND ONE OF THEM CHANGES THE MODEL:** | What you meant | Use | |---|---| | "the soffit height in here", "how high is the ceiling" - to know | `MEASURE_CEILING_HEIGHT`, read-only | | "line up the soffits", "align the undersides" - to change | `ALIGN_ELEMENTS` with an edge, which MOVES services | Asking a height must never move a duct. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="copy-elements"></a>

### Copy elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** duplicate these elements at an offset or copy them up onto other levels, one copy per level, and hand back the copies.

Duplicates every element at one offset and hands back the NEW elements, so the next step can act on the copies alone - select just them, set a parameter on just them, move just them. Or onto other levels, as Paste Aligned to Selected Levels does: one copy on each level named in toLevels, each belonging to that level, optionally turned a further turnDegrees per level about turnCentreMm. Version 5 copies round a point too - count in all across sweepDegrees about turnCentreMm, a full circle divided by the count. Unlike moving and rotating, this one is self-evidencing: Revit returns the ids it created, and a copy that did not happen is a copy that is not in that list. There is no before-and-after comparison here because there is nothing to compare - the evidence arrives with the answer. That is worth saying out loud, because the sibling fragments are full of position probes and their absence here looks like an oversight. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="distribute-along-run"></a>

### Distribute along run

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-14 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put one of these every so many metres along that run.

Places instances of one family at a fixed spacing along a linear element - hangers and supports down a duct run, brackets along a tray, sprinklers off a branch. **Asking for this used to reach ARRAY_ELEMENTS**, which repeats elements that already exist along a direction somebody gives. This takes the direction from the run itself and creates what is not there yet, which is how the request actually arrives: nobody places the first hanger and then arrays it. **THE SPACING IS NOT STRETCHED TO FIT, AND THE REMAINDER IS REPORTED.** A run of 7.3 m at 2 m centres takes three, with 1.3 m left over. Quietly using 1.825 m to come out even is a different instruction from the one given, and it is the kind of helpfulness that puts a support somewhere a drawing says it is not. The leftover is stated so the decision stays with whoever asked. **What is placed is NOT hosted on the run.** These are point-placed instances standing where the run is today. Move the duct and they stay behind. Revit's own hanger families work the same way and it surprises people every time, so it is said in the read-back rather than discovered later. **An end offset keeps the first and last off the joints.** A hanger exactly on a fitting is not buildable, and starting flush with the end is almost never what anybody means. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a run full of hangers is one undo.

<a id="fillet-lines"></a>

### Fillet lines

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-17 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** round the corner between two drafting lines to a radius.

Rounds the corner between exactly TWO model or detail lines with a true tangent arc at a given radius: both lines are cut back to their tangent points and an arc is drawn between them. **"Fillet" means two different operations in Revit, and only one of them is this.** On drafting lines it is geometry - a radius somebody chooses. On a duct or a pipe it is a real ELBOW FITTING, whose shape comes from the type's routing preferences and not from any radius that could be typed. The earlier library carried both in one file behind a mode switch; here the MEP half is already FIT_MEP_JOINTS, so this fragment is the drafting half alone and refuses MEP curves by name rather than doing something plausible to them. **THE TWO SOURCE LINES ARE DELETED AND REDRAWN, SO THEY COME BACK WITH NEW IDS.** That is not tidiness - it is the only thing that works. Editing a line in place to shorten it has been seen to do nothing at all when the two lines already share an endpoint, which is exactly the corner this fragment exists to round: no exception, a clean commit, and the original geometry still there on re-read. Delete and redraw is reliable where the in-place edit is not, and the cost is that anything holding the old ids - a saved set, a tag, a dimension - is holding ids that no longer exist. The new ids are reported. **A radius too large for the lines is refused with the length it would need.** The tangent point has to fall on both lines; a radius that pushes it past the end has no fillet, and the number needed to correct it is more use than a refusal on its own. **A corner of about 0 or about 180 degrees is refused.** There is nothing to round in a straight line or a fold-back, and the arithmetic there produces a huge arc rather than an error. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16) - which matters more here than usual, because the delete and the redraw must be one undo step or a failure halfway leaves two lines gone and no arc.

<a id="find-nearest-elements"></a>

### Find nearest elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which one of those is closest to each of these.

For each element, the nearest one from a second set. "Which FCU serves this terminal", "which exit is closest to this room", "what is the nearest light to each switch". With withinMm, every one within that distance too, nearest first (version 2). **THREE WAYS TO MEASURE DISTANCE, AND THE CHOICE CHANGES THE ANSWER**, so it is a request input rather than a default: | `metric` | What it measures | When it is right | |---|---|---| | `centre` | straight line between centres | point-like equipment; **misleading for long elements** - a 30 m wall's centre can be far away while the wall runs right past you | | `gap` | closest approach between the two boxes, 0 if they overlap | real clearance, and the honest answer to "how close is that to this" | | `manhattan` | the three axis distances added | cable, conduit and duct do not fly diagonally through a building - for "how much cable will this take" this is far closer to reality than a straight line | Picking one silently would answer a different question from the one asked, and all three are defensible. **IT MEASURES PROXIMITY, NOT DIRECTION OR CONNECTION.** The nearest FCU to a terminal is not necessarily the one serving it, and the nearest exit may be through a wall. This narrows a search; it does not establish a relationship, and `TRACE_CONNECTIVITY` is what answers what is actually joined to what. **THE GAP FIGURE IS OPTIMISTIC ON A ROTATED ELEMENT AND MUST NOT BE QUOTED AS A CLEARANCE.** Bounding boxes are axis-aligned, so a rotated element's box is bigger than the element and two of them appear closer than they are. That is fine for ranking - the ordering is what this is for - and wrong for a certified figure. **IT NEEDS TWO SETS OF ELEMENTS AND ONLY ONE OF THEM CAN BE CALLED `elements`.** The things to measure FROM and the things to measure TO are both what a filter provides, so `targets` declares `binds: elements` - fill me from a provide called `elements`. The host runs the filter twice, once per role. Naming it `targets` rather than reusing `elements` is the point: which set is which decides the whole answer, and a contract that could not say so would make the two interchangeable on paper while they are not. **A TIE IS RETURNED AS A TIE.** Two candidates at the same distance is a real situation, and picking one on id order would make the answer depend on the order Revit happens to hand them back. **MILLIMETRES OUT, BY MULTIPLYING BY 304.8**, the same as MEASURE_DISTANCE - which is the fragment a modeller reaches for next, with the pair this one found. `distances` used to leave here in Revit's internal FEET under a bare name, so the two answered "how far apart" 304.8x apart from each other. The comparisons are still done in feet, because that is what a bounding box is in; only the number that leaves is converted, and its name now carries the unit the way every other converted length in this library does.

<a id="measure-ceiling-height"></a>

### Measure ceiling height

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how much clear height there is under the ceiling in each room.

Which ceilings sit over each room, how high the underside of each one is above the floor, and which of them is the one a person means by "the ceiling height". The number every service above the ceiling depends on - duct depth, sprinkler drop, FCU space, the light fitting recess. **A ROOM USUALLY HAS MORE THAN ONE CEILING, AND "THE CEILING HEIGHT" MEANS THE MAIN ONE.** A bulkhead, a soffit over the joinery and the main grid are three ceilings over one room at three heights. Taking the first one found is how a report quotes a 400 mm bulkhead as the room's ceiling height. The main ceiling here is the one covering the most of the room in plan, and **every ceiling found is returned with its own height** so the drop and the bulkhead are both visible rather than averaged away. **THE HEIGHT IS READ FROM THE CEILING'S OWN PARAMETER, NOT FROM GEOMETRY.** Height-above-level plus the level's elevation is exact, cheap, and is the number Revit itself shows. Deriving it from a solid would give a second figure that disagrees with the Properties palette in the last decimal, and two numbers that both look right is worse than one that is plainly wrong. **IT USES `ProjectElevation`, WHICH IS THE HALF OF THIS THAT GOES WRONG SILENTLY.** A level has two heights and only one is in the same space as the model's coordinates. On a site model with a survey offset the other one is wrong by exactly that offset, with a plausible number. `REPORT_LEVEL_ELEVATIONS` says whether this model is affected. **WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, AND WHY THAT IS DELIBERATE.** The obvious alternative is to intersect the room's solid with the ceilings. A room's solid stops at its Upper Limit, which on a great many real models is left just above the room's own level - so the solid stops BELOW the ceiling and intersects nothing, and the report says "no ceiling" for a room that plainly has one. The known workaround is to raise the upper limit, measure, and roll it back. **A fragment here may not do that.** Golden Rule 16 means a fragment runs inside a transaction it did not open and must not open one, so a change and a rollback would land inside somebody else's batch and take its undo entry with it. A read that quietly writes is worse than a read that returns less. The plan-overlap test below needs no room solid and so never meets the trap at all.

**"SOFFIT" MEANS TWO DIFFERENT JOBS AND ONE OF THEM CHANGES THE MODEL:** | What you meant | Use | |---|---| | "the soffit height in here", "how high is the ceiling" - to know | `MEASURE_CEILING_HEIGHT`, read-only | | "line up the soffits", "align the undersides" - to change | `ALIGN_ELEMENTS` with an edge, which MOVES services | Asking a height must never move a duct. Both fragments carry this table: a cross-reference written one way only routes whoever lands on the newer file, and which one a search returns is not something either of them chooses. **THE COST OF THAT CHOICE, STATED:** the overlap is measured on axis-aligned bounding boxes, so a rotated room over-reports how much of it a ceiling covers, and ranking by plan area rather than by intersected volume can pick differently from a solid test where a large thin soffit competes with a smaller main grid. `coverage` is returned per ceiling so a close call is visible instead of decided in silence. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link's ceilings are measured the same way - their own height above their own level - carried through each placement into this model's space and tested against each room or space by the same plan-overlap rule, and `linkedMatches` gives each room's main linked ceiling: clear height in millimetres, coverage and type. An MEP model's spaces sit under ceilings it does not contain, so this is the answer a host-only run cannot give. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - every dictionary stays this model's own, because they are keyed and valued by ids the next step looks up here (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="measure-distance"></a>

### Measure distance

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** how far apart are these two.

Reports how far apart two elements are - the straight-line distance, and the horizontal and vertical parts of it separately, in millimetres. **Asking how far apart two things are used to reach FIND_NEAREST_ELEMENTS**, which finds the nearest one and does not measure. That was measured. A finder and a measure are different jobs, and the question here already knows which two elements it is about. **Three numbers, because a modeller needs all three.** The straight-line distance is what a tape measure gives; the horizontal distance is what a plan drawing shows; the vertical is the one that decides whether a duct clears a beam. Reporting only the first makes the reader do trigonometry to get the other two, and they are what the question was usually about. **The distance is measured between the two nearest points of the elements' bounding boxes, and the report says so.** An element is not a point: a thirty-metre duct has no single position, and measuring centre to centre would call two touching runs thirty metres apart. Where both are point-placed the two definitions agree, and the report still names which was used. **Touching or overlapping elements report zero**, which is a real answer and not a failure. FIND_CLASHES is what says whether they overlap. **Millimetres out, by multiplying by 304.8.** Internal feet are not what anybody asked, and stating the unit in the answer is what stops a number being read as the wrong one.

<a id="measure-perimeter"></a>

### Measure perimeter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-19 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** how far is it round the edge of this.

Measures the perimeter of each element given - the distance round its boundary - and totals them. **AREA, VOLUME AND LENGTH WERE ALL COVERED AND PERIMETER WAS NOT.** `REPORT_AREAS`, `MEASURE_ELEMENT_VOLUME` and `MEASURE_RUN_QUANTITIES` answer the other three. Perimeter appears in this library only INSIDE `REPORT_DUCT_WEIGHT` and `MEASURE_RUN_QUANTITIES`, as sheet-metal arithmetic on a duct section, and never as a number anybody can ask for about a room or a floor. It is what skirting, coving, edge trim and kerb are all measured in. **A ROOM'S PERIMETER IS REVIT'S OWN, NOT A SUM OF SEGMENTS.** Rooms carry `ROOM_PERIMETER`, computed against the same boundary rules the area uses. Adding up boundary segments instead gives a different number wherever a boundary location setting is not at the wall centre, and it would disagree with the room schedule on the same sheet. **EVERYTHING ELSE IS MEASURED FROM ITS FOOTPRINT.** For a floor, a ceiling or a filled region the perimeter is the length round the largest horizontal face, and holes in it are NOT added - somebody asking for the perimeter of a slab wants the outside, and the count of faces skipped says how many there were. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="mirror-elements"></a>

### Mirror elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** mirror these elements across a vertical plane.

Mirrors elements across a vertical plane drawn through two points in plan - the usual job being a room laid out as the reflection of the one next door. It can mirror in place or leave the originals and produce mirrored copies. The copy mode is the safer one and the one that composes: it hands back the new ids, so the next step can work on the reflection alone. **Mirroring CONNECTED MEP in place does not do what it looks like.** Revit keeps the connections and re-fits the geometry around them, so a duct run mirrored without its fittings comes back as a constrained shape rather than a reflection. Include the fittings, or mirror as a copy. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="offset-elements"></a>

### Offset elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** shift each linear run sideways by a perpendicular distance.

Moves each linear run sideways by a perpendicular distance, in plan - a parallel duct beside an existing one, a pipe moved clear of a wall. Unlike a plain move it follows the run: an already-curved run stays parallel to itself rather than being translated. **Offsetting a connected MEP run breaks its connections.** The geometry moves and the fittings do not follow, so the run comes apart at every joint. That is Revit's behaviour rather than this fragment's, and the answer is to reconnect afterwards or to offset the whole run including its fittings. In place only. A parallel COPY is COPY_ELEMENTS followed by this - which is the composition working, and is why there is no copy mode here. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="plan-connection-order"></a>

### Plan connection order

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what order should I connect these in.

Works out the cheapest way to connect a loose set of elements and reports the ORDER, the links and the total run length. *"Which order do I wire these forty fittings in"*, *"chain these terminals off that unit"*, *"how much cable is this"*. **NOTHING ELSE IN THIS LIBRARY DECIDES AN ORDER, AND TWO FRAGMENTS ALREADY DEPEND ON ONE.** CREATE_MEP_RUNS consumes points that are already sequenced and RENUMBER_SEQUENTIAL states outright that it does not choose the order. Both currently need a human to supply the sequence they eat. This computes it. **IT COMPUTES AND DRAWS NOTHING.** The earlier version of this idea also drew the route into a view, which meant one fragment doing an optimisation and a drafting job. The answer here is data - an order, a set of links, a length - and drawing it is a separate decision with its own traps about model versus detail lines. Splitting them is also what makes this safe to run on a whole floor to see the number. **A TREE AND A CHAIN ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS AND ONLY ONE OF THEM GIVES AN ORDER.** A tree connects everything with the least total length and is allowed to branch - which is how a real homerun behaves, splitting to serve several fittings. It has no sequence, so `order` comes back EMPTY for it and `links` carries the answer. A chain is one continuous run visiting each element once, which is what a sequence means. Handing a tree result to something expecting an order is the mistake this separation exists to make impossible. **THE GUARANTEES ARE DIFFERENT AND THE FRAGMENT SAYS WHICH APPLIES.** The tree is exact - it IS the shortest total for the distances given. The chain is a heuristic, nearest-neighbour improved by repeated pair-swapping, usually within a few percent and never guaranteed, because the exact version of that problem has no fast solution. `guarantee` carries the word, so nothing downstream claims "shortest possible" for a chain. **UNGROUPED, IT DOES NOT KNOW WALLS EXIST.** Nearest-neighbour will hop into the next room because a fitting there is 200 mm closer and then come back, which nobody would ever pull cable like. Passing `groupKeys` routes each room or zone as its own run and then links the runs together - local runs, feeders between them, which is the real shape of distribution. **EXPECT GROUPING TO REPORT A LONGER TOTAL AND DO NOT TREAT THAT AS A REGRESSION.** Grouping is a constraint - finish this room before leaving it - and constraints cost length. The ungrouped figure is shorter only because it is cheating: it crosses between zones far more often than anybody would build, which is to say it runs back and forth through walls. **The ungrouped number is unbuildable and the grouped number is the real one.** **THE CONTINUOUS MODE CHOOSES WHERE EACH GROUP ENDS, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE IDEA.** Finishing a room and then jumping to the nearest fitting in any room not yet done is obvious. What is not obvious is that the EXIT should not be accepted, it should be optimised: every candidate last-fitting in the room is tried, and the one that minimises the path through the room PLUS the jump out of it wins. That one change is the difference between a grouped route that costs a quarter more than the unbuildable ideal and one that lands within a few per cent of it. **THE LENGTHS ARE ESTIMATES AND THE MEASURE IS AN INPUT, BECAUSE CABLE DOES NOT FLY.** Point to point in a straight line is a LOWER BOUND that can never be achieved. Orthogonal distance - across, along and up - assumes running square along ceilings and down walls, which is far closer to how it is actually installed, and it is the one to use unless a lower bound is specifically wanted. Neither knows about obstructions, trays, or a drop nobody modelled. **This is the right connection ORDER plus a sensible length estimate. It is not a cable schedule.** ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none, needs none and changes nothing.

<a id="probe-around-elements"></a>

### Probe around elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** what is around this thing, and how far away.

Fires rays out of each element in the directions asked for and reports what each one hits and how far away. The look before a move: what is above this duct, what is beside this pump, how much room is there. **RAYS ONLY SEE WHAT THE 3D VIEW SHOWS, AND NOTHING WARNS YOU.** Ray casting runs inside a 3D view and obeys it completely - hidden categories, section boxes, view filters, closed worksets. A view with walls switched off reports a clear path with a wall standing in it. Proven in a real model: the same element, the same ray, 0 neighbours in one view and 4 in another. The view is a request input for that reason, and the first thing to check when a result looks impossibly empty. **THE DISTANCE IS FROM THE ELEMENT'S POINT, NOT ITS FACE.** The ray starts at the insertion point, inside the element, so a 600 mm deep unit reports about 300 mm less clearance than a tape would. It is a real number measured from a stated place, and reading it as face-to-face is how a clearance passes on paper and fails on site. **ONE RAY PER DIRECTION MISSES THINGS BESIDE A BIG ELEMENT.** A single ray from the centre sees only what is directly in line with it: a pipe passing the corner of an air handling unit is invisible to it. For anything large, probe from several points rather than trusting one. **A HIT ON THE ELEMENT ITSELF IS DROPPED.** The ray starts inside its own geometry, so its own faces are the first thing in the way. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none. **LINKED MODELS ARE PROBED ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, each direction is cast a second time with Revit's own FindReferencesInRevitLinks, and where the nearest thing within reach is in a LINK - the architect's wall, the structural beam - it gets a line in `linkedMatches` with the linked element's type, id IN THE LINK, Fire Rating and distance in millimetres. Where something in this model is nearer, the host answer already has it. **The same view rule holds**: a link hidden in the view is not seen. `linksSearched` says how many links are loaded: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `hits`, `nothingHit` and `noOrigin` stay this model's answer (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Only model elements are read from a link, never its views or sheets. Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

<a id="read-ceiling-grid"></a>

### Read ceiling grid

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the tile size of this ceiling, and where its grid starts.

Reads a ceiling's real tile size out of its surface pattern - never assuming 600 x 600 - and offers a starting point for the grid. It reports `anchorIsGuessed` as its own answer, and that flag is the whole reason this is a separate fragment. Revit stores the tile SIZE but not where the grid actually STARTS: the interactive ceiling tools ask a person to click a grid intersection for exactly that reason. Without one, this uses a corner of the ceiling and produces centres that are evenly spaced and PARALLEL to the real grid - but possibly half a tile out from what is drawn on screen. Nothing about that fails loudly. It lands on a neat, wrong grid. So the uncertainty is returned as data rather than buried, and whatever snaps things is expected to pass it on to the user.

<a id="read-room-geometry"></a>

### Read room geometry

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** the shape, area and height of one room or space.

Reads the outline, area and height of one Room or Space, so a layout job has something real to lay out inside. It is the first step of every "how many fit in here, and where" question - air terminals, sprinkler heads, detectors. KIND: `action`, NOT `filter`, and the distinction is D-29's rather than a convenience. A filter answers *which elements*. This answers *what is true of this one*, which is the shape `read-element-parameters` already has. It was written as a filter first, and the orphan check reported it as one nothing can consume. That report was right about the fact and wrong about the cause: nothing consumes it because what it produces is consumed by the CALLER, not by another fragment. Turning an outline and a spacing into a list of points is arithmetic, and arithmetic between two Revit calls belongs to the Orchestrator - which is the host (D-01, docs/02 s4), not this library. The label was corrected; the composition was never the problem. It reports `unbounded` and `heightKnown` as separate facts rather than folding either into a zero. An unbounded room returns an area of 0 from Revit, and a layout that trusts that number places nothing and reports success. **IT DOES NOT MEASURE THE ROOM, AND IT USED TO CLAIM THE SENTENCES THAT ASK IT TO.** This hands back an outline for something else to lay out inside: | What you meant | Use | |---|---| | "how many fit in here", "lay them out in this space" | **this fragment** | | "how big is this room", "what are the room sizes" | `REPORT_ROOM_SPACE_DATA` | It carried *"how big is this room"* and *"what is the room size"* until `MEASURE_ROOM_DIMENSIONS` existed, and answering those with a list of curves was never what they meant. They moved because the other fragment is genuinely the better answer - not to buy back a rank, which is the one move `brain/retrieval-history.md` rules out. **VERSION 2 SEPARATES THE HOLES FROM THE OUTLINE, AND VERSION 1 DID NOT.** A room's boundary comes back as a list of LOOPS: the first is the outside edge and every one after it is a hole - a core, a shaft, a column the room wraps around. Version 1 flattened them all into one list, so a layout built on it treated the shaft's edge as part of the room's outline. Nothing had noticed, because a room without a hole in it - which is most rooms - gives the same answer either way. `holes` is now its own list, and a caller that ignores it is at worst where it was before.

| **You get** | boundary, holes, hole loops, area, height, unbounded, height known |

<a id="report-areas"></a>

### Report areas

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the Areas in this model, per scheme, because schemes overlap on purpose.

Reports AREAS - the Area-plan kind, not Rooms - broken down by Area Scheme and by level, with a total per scheme. Gross, rentable, common-area: the numbers a landlord, a cost plan or a submission asks for. It changes nothing. **AREAS ARE A THIRD SPATIAL ELEMENT AND NOTHING HERE COVERED THEM.** This library has Rooms and Spaces thoroughly - `PLACE_ROOMS`, `REPORT_ROOM_SPACE_DATA`, `READ_ROOM_GEOMETRY`, `READ_SPACE_LOADS`, `FILTER_ELEMENTS_IN_ROOM` - and `OST_Areas` appeared in none of them. Asking a room fragment for an area answer gets a confidently wrong number. Measured before this batch, *"report the areas in this model"* resolved to `REPORT_LEVEL_ELEVATIONS`. **THE SCHEMES OVERLAP ON PURPOSE, AND THAT IS WHY THERE IS NO GRAND TOTAL.** The same floor is measured twice - once under Gross Building and once under Rentable - and both sets of Area elements sit in `OST_Areas` at the same time, in the same place. Collect the category and sum it and the total is roughly double the building and belongs to no scheme at all. **Every number here is per scheme, and a total across schemes is deliberately not offered**, because such a total has no meaning and would be believed. **UNPLACED AND UNBOUNDED BOTH READ AS ZERO AND HAVE DIFFERENT FIXES**, so they are separated: | State | What is true | What to do | |---|---|---| | **Unplaced** | the Area exists in the schedule but sits nowhere in the model | place it, or delete the row | | **Unbounded** | it IS placed, but its boundary lines do not close | close the boundary | Both occupy a row in every area schedule and contribute nothing to the total. A report that shows them as "0" alongside real areas hides the difference, and the difference is the whole fix.

<a id="report-bounding-box"></a>

### Report bounding box

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** the box each element occupies, and the box the whole set occupies.

The extent each element occupies - its size and its lowest corner, in mm - plus the single box that contains the whole set. It changes nothing. IT EXISTS BECAUSE *"what is the bounding box of this duct"* RESOLVED TO `FILTER_ELEMENTS_IN_ROOM`, and *"how big is the box around these elements"* to `SET_VIEW_SECTION_BOX` - a filter and a view setting, for a measurement. **THE BOX IS ALIGNED TO PROJECT X AND Y, AND THAT IS THE ONE THING TO KNOW BEFORE USING THE NUMBER.** It is not the element's own size. For anything running square to the project it is the same thing; for anything at an angle it is bigger than the object, in a shape the object does not have. | Asking about | Use | |---|---| | A duct, a pipe, a piece of equipment - **how much space does it take** | here | | A **room** - how big is it | `REPORT_ROOM_SPACE_DATA`, which measures on the room's own axes | | **How much material** is in it | `MEASURE_ELEMENT_VOLUME` - solid volume and surface area | `REPORT_ROOM_SPACE_DATA` carries this same table and states the case in numbers: turn an 8000 x 4000 room thirty degrees and its box becomes roughly 8900 x 7500. **This fragment is the right answer to "what space does it occupy" and the wrong answer to "how big is it".** **THE COMBINED BOX IS THE USEFUL HALF FOR COORDINATION.** *"Will this plant fit through that opening"*, *"how deep is the services zone"*, *"where do I put the section box"* are all one question about a set, not a list of boxes. It is reported whether or not the per-element list is truncated. **AN ELEMENT WITH NO BOX IS REPORTED, NOT SKIPPED.** A view-specific element, an empty group or a purely annotation element has none. Skipping them silently makes the combined box look like it covers everything asked about.

<a id="report-centroid"></a>

### Report centroid

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-19 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** where is the middle of this, by volume rather than by its box.

Reports each element's centroid - the centre of its actual volume - and the combined centroid of the whole set. **`REPORT_BOUNDING_BOX` GIVES THE BOX AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT NUMBER.** The centre of an axis-aligned box is not the centre of the thing inside it, and for anything L-shaped, sloped or rotated the two are far apart - the box's centre can sit in fresh air outside the element entirely. Measured 2026-09-18, the only centroid in the whole library is computed inside `CENTER_ROOM_TAGS` for tag placement and never handed back. **THE COMBINED CENTROID IS WEIGHTED BY VOLUME, NOT BY COUNT.** Averaging the centroids treats a bolt and a beam as equals and gives an answer that is not the centre of anything. Weighting by volume is what makes it a centre of mass for a set of the same material - and because it is only that when the material is the same, the finding says so rather than letting somebody read it as one. **AN ELEMENT WITH NO SOLID IS COUNTED, NOT GUESSED AT.** Annotation, most analytical elements and an unplaced room have no volume, so they have no centroid; giving them their bounding box centre instead would quietly mix two different measurements in one answer. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="report-door-room-links"></a>

### Report door room links

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-21 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** which room each door leads from and to, checked against the geometry.

Says which room each door leads FROM and TO - and checks Revit's own answer against where the rooms physically are. It changes nothing. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTION WAS BEING ANSWERED BY `PLACE_ROOMS`.** Measured before this batch, *"what rooms are on either side of this door"* resolved to the fragment that CREATES ROOMS - a read question answered by putting elements in the model. **`FromRoom` AND `ToRoom` ARE DECIDED BY THE DOOR'S FACING, NOT BY THE ROOMS.** This is the whole reason the fragment is more than two lines. Flip a door in the model and the two swap - the plan still looks right, the schedule reads backwards, and nothing warns you. So each one is CHECKED: take a point a short way either side of the door along its own facing normal and ask each room whether the point is inside it. **Where the geometry disagrees with the property, the geometry wins and the disagreement is REPORTED, never silently corrected** - a flipped door is a modelling problem worth knowing about, not just a reporting one. That is this project's standing rule in a new place: Revit's own data describes INTENT, and intent and physical reality come apart. `TRACE_CONNECTIVITY` exists for the same reason on the MEP side. **FROM AND TO ARE PHASE-DEPENDENT, AND THE BARE PROPERTY ANSWERS FOR THE LAST PHASE ONLY.** On a refurbishment - where the room on either side of a door is exactly what changes - the bare property is wrong for every phase but one. The phase actually used is named in every row, so a reader can see which answer they were given. **A DOOR WITH ONE ROOM IS CORRECT, NOT A FAILURE.** An entrance door has outside on one side. That is reported as `(outside)`. A door with NEITHER side in a room is a different thing - usually rooms not placed or not enclosed - and is reported as that. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as version 1 did. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. Every door in each link is checked against that link's own rooms, on its phase of the same name, and reported in `linkedMatches` - a selection cannot reach a linked door. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - the counts and lists stay this model's own doors; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer.

A bounding-box centre is always named as a fallback, never as a location.

<a id="rotate-elements"></a>

### Rotate elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** turn these elements about a vertical axis, and check they really turned.

Turns every element about a vertical axis - a mis-oriented piece of equipment spun 90 degrees, a cluster of terminals turned to match a new room layout. Like moving, and for the same reason: Revit's rotate call returns normally and rotates NOTHING for a pinned element or a group member. Five grouped air terminals stayed at 0.00 degrees while the code reported *"rotated 5, skipped 0"*. So orientation is read before and after, and only a change in it counts. The pivot may be left out, and then each element turns about its own position - which is what *"spin that damper round"* means, as against *"swing this whole row about the corner"*. Since version 3 it really can be: left out, it reads as none. Version 2 turns about any line given as well - `axisLine` - so a panel can tilt; a zero angle is refused, and Revit refusing outright is kept apart from an element that did not move. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | rotated, rotated ids, findings |

4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"rotate the equipment 90 degrees"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
5. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"spin that damper round"* · *"turn them to face the other way"*

<a id="snap-to-grid"></a>

### Snap to grid

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** move each element sideways onto the nearest cell centre of a grid.

Moves each point-based element sideways onto the nearest CELL CENTRE of a grid it is given - diffusers, sprinklers, light fittings and detectors sitting neatly on the ceiling grid instead of somewhere in the room. **Plan move only.** Every element keeps its own height, because the two jobs are separate: this puts things in the right place on the ceiling, and MOVE_TO_RAY_HIT puts them at the right height. A real layout usually wants both, in that order, and merging them would make it impossible to do one without the other. It takes the grid as numbers rather than reading it from a ceiling. That is what makes it usable for any grid - a setting-out grid, a structural bay, a raised-floor grid - and it is why the ceiling half is its own capability. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | snapped |

### Straighten off axis lines

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** straighten these lines that are slightly off axis so the warning goes.

Turns walls, grids, model and detail lines, reference planes, room separation and area boundary lines that lie a fraction of a degree off an axis exactly onto it, clearing Revit's "slightly off axis" warnings.

<a id="trim-extend-elements"></a>

### Trim extend elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make these two lines meet cleanly at a corner.

Takes exactly TWO straight elements and moves each one's nearer end to the point where their directions cross, so they meet at one clean corner. It trims where they overran and extends where they fell short - the same operation either way, which is why it is one fragment and not two. Works on anything with a straight line location: duct, pipe, cable tray, conduit, wall, model line, detail line. **The corner is solved in plan, and that is a limit, not an oversight.** Two runs at the same height square off correctly; two that are skew in three dimensions have no single corner, and a vertical riser turning into a horizontal run is not this operation. The Z of each element is left as it was. **THE RESULT IS READ BACK FROM THE MODEL, because writing it is not proof it took.** Reassigning a location curve in place has been seen to do nothing at all for two drafting lines that ALREADY shared an endpoint - no exception, the transaction commits, and re-reading the element gives the original geometry back. Rather than trust a fix that was never tested for this operation, this re-reads both elements afterwards and reports **where each end actually landed**. A move that silently did not happen shows up as a stated failure instead of a success message. **Two parallel lines are refused.** There is no corner to meet at, and inventing one is worse than saying so. **This breaks MEP connections at the ends it moves.** A duct dragged off its neighbour is disconnected, and Revit does not put it back. FIT_MEP_JOINTS joins the new corner with a real elbow, which is usually the next step. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). The earlier version of this opened its own, which would have made a batch several undo steps instead of one.
